name: Battle of Grathe Heath
location: Grathe Heath in central Jutland, near Hauge Sø south of Silkeborg
summary: The battle of 23 October 1157 in which Valdemar destroyed Sweyn III, eleven weeks after Sweyn had tried to murder him at the Bloodfeast of Roskilde. Sweyn was caught in flight and killed by peasants, ending twenty-six years of Danish civil war and opening the Valdemarian age.
details: Sweyn III had sprung his trap at the reconciliation feast in Roskilde on 9 August 1157, killing Canute V; Valdemar escaped wounded to Jutland and raised it against him. Sweyn brought his Zealand and Scanian forces across and the two met on the heath at Grathe. His army broke, and he was taken in the marshy ground in flight and killed on the spot. Valdemar became sole king, reigned for twenty-five years with Absalon beside him, and founded the dynasty that made Denmark the dominant power in the Baltic.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: On 23 October 1157 Valdemar, son of the murdered Canute Lavard, beat and killed King Sweyn III on Grathe Heath in central Jutland. It was the last battle of a civil war that had begun with a killing in a wood in 1131 and had run through five reigns, three simultaneous kings and one massacre at a dinner table.

The battle followed directly from that massacre. In July 1157 the three rivals — Sweyn III, Canute V and Valdemar — had agreed to divide Denmark between them and to seal the partition at a feast of reconciliation in Roskilde. On 9 August, at the feast, Sweyn’s men attacked the other two. Canute V was killed outright; Valdemar, wounded, cut his way out and rode for Jutland.

Grathe Heath is therefore not a battle of manoeuvre but a verdict. Jutland rose for the man who had been the victim of a broken oath, and the sources present the outcome as the punishment of treachery. Since the fullest of those sources was written a generation later under the patronage of Valdemar’s closest friend, that framing is worth naming for what it is.

contentSections.title: Three kings and a partition
paragraphs: Denmark had been fought over since Magnus the Strong murdered Canute Lavard in 1131 and lost the resulting war at Fotevik in 1134. Eric II was murdered at an assembly in 1137; his nephew Eric III ruled uneasily and then abdicated in 1146, the only medieval Danish king to resign the crown, and entered a monastery at Odense, where he died the following year.

His abdication left no agreed heir and produced two at once. Sweyn, son of Eric II, was elected in Scania and Zealand; Canute, son of Magnus the Strong, was raised up in Jutland. Valdemar, the posthumous son of Canute Lavard, was a boy and became the third party to the quarrel as he grew. The war that followed drew in the German emperor: at Merseburg in 1152 Frederick Barbarossa arbitrated between the claimants and awarded the kingdom to Sweyn, with Zealand to Canute, and it held for barely a year.

By 1157 all three were exhausted, and the partition agreed that summer was an admission that none could win: Sweyn took Scania, Canute Zealand, Valdemar Jutland. It was to be confirmed at Roskilde over dinner.

contentSections.title: The Bloodfeast of Roskilde
paragraphs: The feast was held on 9 August 1157. According to the account Saxo Grammaticus set down about forty years later, Sweyn had planned the attack in advance; the lights were put out and armed men came in. Canute V was cut down where he sat. Valdemar took a wound to the thigh and fought his way to the door with Absalon, his foster-brother, and got clear of the town.

The political effect was immediate and total. A killing at a feast of reconciliation, under oath and under a roof where guests had been received, broke the one rule that made negotiated settlements possible in a war of this kind. Men who had accepted Sweyn as king were released from the reasons they had for doing so.

Valdemar reached Jutland, had his wound treated and raised the province. Sweyn had to follow him: leaving a wounded claimant in possession of Jutland with a fresh grievance was not a settlement he could live with.

contentSections.title: The battle on the heath
paragraphs: The armies met on Grathe Heath, open ground in central Jutland beside Hauge Sø, north of what is now Thorning. Sweyn had brought his forces from Zealand and Scania into a province that had gone over to his enemy, and the fighting was short. His army broke and ran.

Sweyn did not get away. He was caught in the wet ground during the flight and killed by local peasants — the detail on which the Danish sources agree and dwell, because a king of Denmark being knocked off a bogged horse and killed by farmers made the point about broken oaths better than any sentence could. He was about thirty-two.

No source gives the size of either army, and none describes the fighting as a sequence of events. What survives is the shape of the day and its ending, which is characteristic of Danish battle-writing in this century: the annals record who died and the chronicles record what it meant.

contentSections.title: Valdemar I and Absalon
paragraphs: Valdemar was now sole king at about twenty-six, and he reigned until 1182. The partner in the reign was Absalon, the foster-brother who had got him out of Roskilde: bishop of Roskilde from 1158, archbishop of Lund from 1178, and the man who fortified the fishing village of Havn that became Copenhagen.

Together they turned a kingdom that had spent a generation fighting itself outward against the Wends of the southern Baltic. The temple-fortress at Arkona on Rügen fell in 1168 and its idol of Svantevit was pulled down, which ended the Wendish raiding that had made the Danish coasts unsafe and gave the crown a run of profitable campaigns to bind its magnates to.

The dynasty was secured with the same care. In 1170 at Ringsted, Valdemar had his father Canute Lavard canonised and his own seven-year-old son crowned co-king on the same day — a single ceremony that made the murdered duke a saint, the murdered duke’s descendants the rightful line, and hereditary succession the rule. That son succeeded as Cnut VI without a fight, which in Denmark was the novelty.

contentSections.title: The heath, the chapel and the sources
paragraphs: Sweyn was buried at Grathe, and a chapel was raised on the heath where he fell; its foundations are still traceable and are marked out on the ground today. The byname the sources give him — Sweyn Grathe — is taken from the place he lost, which is an unusual way for a king to be remembered and tells its own story about who wrote the record.

That record is overwhelmingly one work. Saxo Grammaticus wrote the Gesta Danorum at Absalon’s urging and largely on Absalon’s information, and Absalon was standing beside Valdemar at the feast and through the campaign. Saxo is detailed, vivid and hostile to Sweyn, and there is no surviving account from Sweyn’s side to set against him. The short Danish annals confirm the dates and the deaths and nothing else.

What can be checked holds. The Roskilde killing of Canute V, the date of the battle and Sweyn’s death on the field are recorded independently of Saxo in the annal tradition. The reported dialogue, the treachery foreseen and the moralised ending are Saxo’s, and belong to the literature of the Valdemarian court rather than to the evidence for 23 October 1157.

leaders.name: Absalon
leaders.title: Absalon
leaders.note: Valdemar’s foster-brother, later bishop of Roskilde and archbishop of Lund; Saxo, who wrote on his information, places him at Valdemar’s side from the escape at Roskilde through the campaign. No Codex article yet.

strength.display: Unknown; the levies of Jutland, raised after the Roskilde killings
strength.note: Neither Saxo nor the Danish annals give a number for either army. The province’s support, not its size, is what the sources treat as decisive.

strength.display: Unknown; forces brought over from Zealand and Scania
strength.note: No figures survive. Sweyn was fighting in a province that had declared against him, and the sources record the rout rather than the numbers involved in it.

outcome: Decisive victory for Valdemar. Sweyn III was defeated and killed in the flight, ending the civil wars begun in 1131. Valdemar ruled as sole king until 1182 and founded the Valdemarian dynasty that made Denmark a Baltic power.

imageInfo.caption: The Grathe stone, a granite memorial cross raised on the heath where Sweyn III was killed, in a 2008 photograph.
imageInfo.creator: Kim Konnerup
imageInfo.date: 2008 photograph; the stone is a modern memorial to the battle of 1157
imageInfo.note: A modern commemoration standing on the battlefield, not a medieval object. It marks the site of the chapel raised over Sweyn’s grave at Grathe, whose outline is still laid out on the ground beside it, and carries a crown and a sword above the inscription naming the king. sectionImages.caption: The Battle of Grathe Heath as imagined by the Danish artist Lorenz Frølich in an engraving of 1885.
sectionImages.creator: Lorenz Frølich
sectionImages.note: Nineteenth-century Danish national memory, not a record: no medieval depiction of the battle exists, and Frølich supplies the fighting the sources decline to describe. The arms and dress are the artist’s idea of the twelfth century. Public domain.

battleContinuity.label: The same problem, settled in Norway
battleContinuity.reason: Valdemar ended Denmark’s succession war by killing the last rival king, and in 1170 sold Danish recognition of Norway’s boy-king to Erling Skakke for homage over Viken; the Norwegian version of the same war ran on until Sverre Sigurdsson drowned Erling’s son Magnus at Fimreite in 1184.

timeline.title: Eric III abdicates
timeline.description: The only medieval Danish king to resign the crown enters a monastery at Odense, leaving no agreed heir and two immediate claimants.

timeline.title: Two kings elected
timeline.description: Sweyn, son of Eric II, is raised up in Scania and Zealand; Canute, son of Magnus the Strong, is elected in Jutland.

timeline.title: Barbarossa arbitrates at Merseburg
timeline.description: The emperor awards Denmark to Sweyn with Zealand to Canute. The award holds for about a year before the war resumes.

timeline.title: The kingdom divided three ways
timeline.description: Sweyn takes Scania, Canute V Zealand and Valdemar Jutland, an admission that none of the three can win outright.

timeline.title: The Bloodfeast of Roskilde
timeline.description: Sweyn’s men attack the other two kings at the feast meant to seal the partition. Canute V is killed; Valdemar escapes wounded with Absalon.

timeline.title: Jutland rises
timeline.description: Valdemar has his thigh wound treated and raises the province against the king who broke the oath at the feast.

timeline.title: Grathe Heath
timeline.description: Sweyn’s army breaks on the heath beside Hauge Sø; he is caught in the wet ground during the flight and killed by peasants.

timeline.title: Absalon made bishop of Roskilde
timeline.description: Valdemar’s foster-brother takes the see of the town where the ambush had been sprung, and becomes the reign’s second man.

timeline.title: Arkona taken
timeline.description: The Wendish temple-fortress on Rügen falls to Valdemar and Absalon, ending the raiding that had made the Danish coasts unsafe.

timeline.title: A saint and a co-king at Ringsted
timeline.description: Canute Lavard is canonised and Valdemar’s son Cnut crowned co-king in one ceremony, fixing hereditary succession in the Valdemar line.

timeline.title: Valdemar I dies
timeline.description: He dies at Vordingborg after twenty-five years as sole king, and Cnut VI succeeds without a challenge — the first uncontested Danish succession in half a century.
